description: Evidence of class, gender and ethnic inequality across income, health, work and education in the UK.
content_html:
Equality and Inequality in Contemporary UK

Sociologists use a wide range of evidence to map inequality in the UK. Social inequality refers to the unequal distribution of valued resources — income, wealth, health, education and social power — between different groups. The spec asks students to consider evidence of inequality across seven named domains and to understand how inequality is produced and sustained through processes such as discrimination, stereotyping, labelling and scapegoating.

Key Fact

The spec identifies seven key domains where inequality is documented in contemporary UK: income and wealth, education, crime, health, family, work and media representation. Inequality in each domain can be explained by structural factors (class, patriarchy, institutional racism) and by processes operating at the individual and institutional level.

Evidence of Inequality Across Seven Domains

Income and wealth: The distribution of income and wealth in the UK remains highly unequal. The highest-earning households earn many times more than those at the lowest end. ONS data consistently shows that the top fifth of households receive a disproportionate share of total household income. Wealth inequality is even more pronounced: ownership of property and assets is concentrated in relatively few hands.

Education: Children from professional and managerial backgrounds significantly outperform those from working-class backgrounds in national assessments. Private schooling reinforces class-based advantage. Gender gaps have shifted: girls now outperform boys at GCSE and A level in many subjects, but subject choice and occupational destination remain gendered. Some ethnic minority groups face additional barriers linked to cultural deprivation arguments, ethnocentric curriculum content and, in some cases, institutional racism.

Crime: Official statistics show that people from lower socioeconomic backgrounds and from some ethnic minority groups are over-represented in arrest, prosecution and imprisonment data. However, sociologists are careful to note that official crime statistics reflect policing and prosecution patterns as much as actual offending. The moral panic around certain groups — young Black men in relation to knife crime, for example — illustrates how media representations and labelling can amplify perceptions of criminality beyond what the evidence supports.

Health: There are significant and persistent health inequalities by social class in the UK. Life expectancy, infant mortality, mental health outcomes and chronic disease all follow a clear social gradient — the lower a person’s class position, the worse their average health outcomes. Gender and ethnicity intersect with class: women live longer on average but report higher rates of depression; some ethnic minority groups face higher rates of certain conditions partly linked to socioeconomic disadvantage.

Family: Family forms are distributed unequally across class and ethnicity. Lone-parent families are more likely to be in poverty, partly because they depend on a single income and face greater childcare costs. Working-class families are less likely to have access to material resources and social capital that ease family functioning. Research also documents a persistent gender inequality within many families: women continue to carry a disproportionate share of domestic labour and childcare (Oakley’s double shift).

Work: The gender pay gap persists across most sectors. Women are over-represented in part-time and lower-paid “feminised” occupations. The glass ceiling continues to restrict women’s access to senior roles. Some ethnic minority workers face hiring discrimination and are under-represented in higher management despite comparable qualifications.

Media representation: Media representations of different social groups can perpetuate stereotypes. Women are frequently represented in a limited range of roles — domestic, decorative or subordinate to men. Ethnic minority groups have historically been under-represented or negatively stereotyped in mainstream UK media. Working-class people may be represented through negative stereotypes (the “chav”, benefit fraud) that scapegoat them for structural problems. These representations can feed into labelling processes and reinforce prejudice.

Private schooling is one of the most visible mechanisms through which class inequality is reproduced. Around 7% of UK children attend private schools, yet their alumni are consistently over-represented in elite occupations — senior law, medicine, politics, finance and the media. The advantage is not solely academic: private schools provide access to social networks and cultural capital that public schools typically cannot. The informal network of contacts, shared school ties and mutual recognition among privately educated individuals is sometimes described as the “old boys’ network” — a form of social closure that operates to preserve elite advantage across generations.

Fiona Devine’s study Affluent Workers Revisited (1992) examined social class identity and inequality from a different angle. Revisiting the site of Goldthorpe and Lockwood’s 1960s Luton car-plant study, Devine interviewed manual workers and their partners. She found that claims of widespread embourgeoisement — the idea that affluent working-class people had absorbed middle-class values and abandoned class identity — were overstated. Workers retained a strong sense of class identity and resentment at extreme inequality, even as many aspired to consumer goods. Devine’s study is important for Eduqas/WJEC students because it challenges the idea that class inequality has diminished with rising living standards, and demonstrates that class identity and awareness of inequality persist even among relatively well-paid workers.

Gender Inequality: Walby on Patriarchy

Sylvia Walby (1990) argued that patriarchy is not simply a matter of individual discrimination but a structural system operating through six institutions simultaneously: paid work, household production, patriarchal culture, sexuality, male violence and the state. Each structure independently restricts women’s power. The gender pay gap, the double shift, media double standards on women’s behaviour, and under-representation in elected office are all, in Walby’s analysis, expressions of this multi-institutional system. Walby also identified a historical shift from private patriarchy (women controlled directly in the family home) to public patriarchy (women formally included in public life but collectively disadvantaged within it). Contemporary crisis of masculinity debates link changes in the labour market (loss of traditional male manufacturing jobs) to shifts in gender identity, suggesting that patriarchal structures are under pressure even as they persist.

Ethnicity Inequality: Racism and Institutional Racism

Ethnic inequality in the UK operates through both individual prejudice and institutional racism — the systematic disadvantage built into the practices and culture of organisations. The MacPherson Report (1999) applied this concept to the Metropolitan Police following the Stephen Lawrence inquiry. Employment studies using matched CVs have demonstrated that applicants with African or Asian-sounding names receive fewer interview invitations than identical applications with traditionally White British names, suggesting that direct discrimination remains a real factor alongside structural disadvantage.

Government and parliament have attempted to address inequality through legislation. The Equality Act 2010 consolidated earlier legislation (Equal Pay Act, Sex Discrimination Act, Race Relations Act) into a single framework, establishing nine protected characteristics including age, disability, gender reassignment, race, religion or belief, sex and sexual orientation. Employers and service providers are legally prohibited from discriminating on these grounds. Sociologists evaluate the effectiveness of this legislation differently: functionalists may see it as evidence that the system is self-correcting toward meritocracy; Marxists argue that formal legal equality does not address structural economic inequality; feminists point to persistent gaps — especially the gender pay gap — as evidence that legislation alone is insufficient where patriarchal structures remain intact.

Key Fact

Devine’s 1992 restudy found that affluent manual workers retained strong class identities and resentment at extreme inequality, contradicting the embourgeoisement thesis. This shows that class inequality is experienced and felt by workers even when living standards rise — rising wages do not dissolve class identity or awareness of structural unfairness.
exam_tip_html: On a 4-mark Describe question about inequality in the contemporary UK, do not simply list different domains without developing any. The mark scheme rewards sociological vocabulary and explanation of mechanisms: name a domain, state the evidence of inequality, then explain the mechanism using a named concept or theorist. For example: gender inequality in paid work (Walby — glass ceiling, paid-work structure of patriarchy) or class inequality in education (private schooling, social closure, cultural capital). On a 12-mark Evaluate, a Mastering-tier response will compare at least two perspectives on why inequality exists — functionalist (meritocracy, Davis and Moore), Marxist (class exploitation, Devine on class identity) and feminist (Walby on patriarchy) — and reach a supported judgement about which explanation is most convincing.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Inequality in the contemporary UK is documented across seven domains: income and wealth, education, crime, health, family, work and media representation. It is produced and sustained through discrimination, stereotyping, labelling, scapegoating and structural barriers including the glass ceiling and the old boys' network.
  • Fiona Devine's 1992 restudy of affluent workers in Luton found that rising living standards had not dissolved class identity or awareness of inequality, challenging the embourgeoisement thesis. This is a key named study for GCSE Sociology students and illustrates that class remains a felt reality even among relatively well-paid workers.
  • Walby's six structures of patriarchy explain gender inequality as a multi-institutional system; institutional racism explains ethnic inequality as built into organisational practices, not only individual prejudice. Legislation has reduced some forms of discrimination but structural inequalities persist.

practice_questions.text:
Which sociologist's 1992 study revisited affluent workers in Luton and found that embourgeoisement had not occurred?
A) Walby
B) Murray
C) Devine
D) Townsend

practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that institutional racism refers to racism within an organisation or system rather than by individuals alone; 1 mark for explaining that it describes collective failure of an organisation to provide equal treatment because of race, operating through processes, attitudes and behaviour. Example: 'Institutional racism is the collective failure of an organisation to provide an appropriate and professional service to people because of their race, detectable in processes, attitudes and behaviour that amount to discrimination even without deliberate intent by individual employees.'

practice_questions.text: Identify and describe one way the media contributes to inequality in the UK.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying one way (e.g. negative stereotyping of working-class people; under-representation or negative portrayal of ethnic minorities; limited or sexualised representations of women). 2 marks for a developed description: e.g. 'Media representations of working-class people often rely on negative stereotypes — portraying them as scroungers, criminals or socially dysfunctional. These representations can contribute to scapegoating, in which structural problems such as unemployment are blamed on the attitudes and behaviour of working-class individuals rather than on economic inequalities. This labelling process can reinforce existing inequalities by shaping public attitudes and policy responses.'

practice_questions.text: Describe Devine's key findings from her 1992 study of affluent workers.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. Devine revisited Luton workers in the late 1980s, interviewing manual workers and their partners in the same location as Goldthorpe and Lockwood's original 1960s study (1 mark). She did not find evidence to support full embourgeoisement — workers had not absorbed middle-class values and abandoned working-class identity (1 mark). Workers retained a strong sense of class identity and resentment at extreme inequality despite rising living standards and consumer aspirations (1 mark). Many had lost faith in the Labour Party to deliver greater equality, but had not abandoned their sense of class identity or awareness of structural unfairness (1 mark).

practice_questions.text: Discuss the view that class is the most important cause of inequality in modern Britain.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: at least two perspectives developed in detail, both sides of the debate, sustained sociological vocabulary, supported judgement. Supporting the view: class inequality evidenced across domains (income, education, health, work); private schooling and old boys' network as mechanisms of social closure; Devine's finding that class identity persists; Marxist view of structural exploitation by bourgeoisie. Contrasting: feminist view that patriarchy is an independent system — gender inequality persists across all class levels (Walby); evidence of ethnic inequality through institutional racism; functionalist view that unequal outcomes reflect meritocratic differences in talent and effort. Named sociologists throughout. Supported judgement.

Secure: Both sides covered, named sociologists referenced, judgement offered.

Developing: Relevant points but mostly one-sided; some vocabulary; assertive conclusion.

Emerging: Basic points, mostly description, few named sociologists.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate sociological explanations of gender inequality in the contemporary UK.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: full range of relevant arguments. Walby's feminist analysis presented in depth — six structures of patriarchy (paid work: glass ceiling and gender pay gap; household production: double shift; male violence; the state: under-representation); private vs public patriarchy shift. At least two contrasting perspectives developed: functionalist (gender role differences reflect functional specialisation, Parsons on expressive/instrumental roles — not necessarily oppressive); Marxist (gender inequality serves capitalism by dividing the working class and providing unpaid domestic labour, class conflict is fundamental). Evidence weighed: gender pay gap data, women's under-representation in senior roles, persistence of domestic labour inequality. Supported judgement about whether Walby's framework or alternative perspectives best explain gender inequality.

Secure: Walby explained with most arguments, contrasting perspective present, judgement offered.

Developing: Walby described but not evaluated; limited counter-perspective; weak conclusion.

Emerging: Basic description of gender inequality; few named theorists; little evaluation.

knowledge_checks.q: Fiona Devine's 1992 study found that affluent manual workers had retained a strong sense of which of the following?
options: Class identity and resentment at extreme inequality
Faith in the Labour Party to deliver change

knowledge_checks.q: The collective failure of an organisation to provide equal treatment because of race, operating through processes and attitudes rather than just individual prejudice, is called:
The invisible barrier that prevents women from advancing to senior positions in organisations despite formal equality is called the glass _____.
Devine's 1992 study revisited workers at a car plant in _____, originally studied by Goldthorpe and Lockwood in the 1960s.
Match each sociologist to their key contribution to understanding inequality:
right: Six structures of patriarchy through which gender inequality operates across society
Affluent Workers Revisited — class identity persists despite rising wages; embourgeoisement not supported
Functionalist theory that stratification is a meritocratic necessity for role allocation

flashcard_questions.a: The unequal distribution of resources, opportunities and power between social groups based on class, gender, ethnicity or other factors.
An oversimplified, fixed and generalised image applied to all members of a social group, often inaccurate and resistant to change.
Blaming a particular social group for social problems, often deflecting attention from structural causes.
The collective failure of an organisation to provide equal treatment to people because of race, operating through processes and behaviour rather than just individual prejudice.
The invisible barrier that prevents women from advancing to senior positions in organisations despite formal equality.

flashcard_questions.q: What did Devine find in her 1992 study of affluent workers?
flashcard_questions.a: Workers retained class identities and resentment at extreme inequality; embourgeoisement (adopting middle-class values) had not occurred.
The claim that affluent workers adopt middle-class values and lifestyles as their wages rise, dissolving traditional class identity.

flashcard_questions.q: Name Walby's six structures of patriarchy.
flashcard_questions.a: Paid work, household production, patriarchal culture, sexuality, male violence, the state.
When women perform a full working day in paid employment and then carry out the majority of domestic tasks at home.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the old boys' network as a mechanism of class inequality?
flashcard_questions.a: Informal social closure whereby privately educated elites preserve access to top positions through shared contacts and mutual recognition.
The process by which groups restrict access to their privileges to their own members, excluding outsiders.
Sustained, hostile media attention focused on a social group, often exaggerating danger and amplifying perceptions of threat beyond the evidence.

glossary_terms.definition: The unequal distribution of resources, opportunities and power between social groups based on factors such as class, gender, ethnicity, age or disability.
Treating an individual or group less favourably based on a characteristic such as class, gender, ethnicity, age or disability.
An oversimplified, fixed and generalised image or idea applied to all members of a social group, often inaccurate and resistant to change.
The collective failure of an organisation to provide an appropriate and professional service to people because of their race, operating through processes, attitudes and behaviour.
The invisible barrier that prevents women from advancing to senior positions in organisations despite formal equality.
The process by which the working class is said to adopt the attitudes, values and lifestyle of the middle class as their incomes rise.
Sustained, hostile attention focused on a particular social group or problem by the media, often exaggerating danger or social threat.
The process by which certain groups restrict access to privileges or resources to their own members, excluding outsiders.
